extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (introductory 'Book of Proof' readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methods for writing and evaluating elementary mathematical proofs: contradiction, contrapositive, direct, existence/uniqueness, constructive vs non-constructive, biconditionals, equivalence chains, and basic set proofs. Targets typical exercises in an intro proof course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for universally quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction often works well in proving statements of the form ∀x, P(x). The proof set-up involves assuming ¬(∀x, P(x)), which is equivalent to ∃x, ¬P(x), giving a specific x for which ¬P(x) is true and often enough to produce a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how to extract a particular counterexample from ¬∀xP(x) (useful for constructing a contradiction). Example provided: to prove 'for every real x in [0,π/2], sin x + cos x > 1', assume there exists x in [0,π/2] with sin x + cos x ≤ 1 and derive a contradiction. Use algebraic manipulation and known identities (e.g., sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proving a conditional via contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P then Q' by contradiction, begin by assuming ¬(P ⇒ Q), which is equivalent to assuming P and ¬Q. From P and ¬Q derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit outline: 'Proposition If P, then Q. Proof. Suppose P and ¬Q. Therefore ... contradiction.' Example: proving 'if a^2 is even then a is even' begins with assuming a^2 is even and a is not even, then deduce contradiction (a^2 would be odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositive or direct proof when simpler
rubrics_metrics.description: Although proof by contradiction is powerful, it's best to use it only when direct and contrapositive approaches do not seem to work, because contradiction proofs can hide simpler contrapositive proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's advice: look for a simpler contrapositive proof before committing to contradiction. Example: a contradiction proof of 'if a^2 − 2a + 7 is even, then a is odd' essentially performs a contrapositive; a clearer approach is to prove the contrapositive directly ('suppose a is not odd, i.e., even, then a^2 − 2a + 7 is odd').

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining proof techniques (proofs within proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex proofs often combine different techniques inside a single proof; for example a direct proof may contain an inner proof by contradiction or contrapositive to establish a subclaim R needed to deduce Q from P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to nest proofs: the overall structure can be direct while subclaims use contradiction, contrapositive, or other methods. Example: proving every nonzero rational number is a product of two irrationals uses a direct outer proof and an inner contradiction to show an auxiliary number is irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for If-and-Only-If proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'P if and only if Q' you must prove both P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P (the converse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: present a proof of P ⇒ Q (using direct/contrapositive/contradiction as appropriate), then begin a new paragraph for the converse, ideally starting with 'Conversely', and prove Q ⇒ P. Example: proving 'n is odd iff n^2 is odd' by direct proof one way and contrapositive the other. Reminder: begin a new paragraph when starting the proof of the converse to aid reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equivalence among several statements (equivalent statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a list of statements are equivalent, prove a series of conditional implications so the statements form a cycle (or use another pattern that connects all statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A circular chain of implications (a⇒b⇒c⇒...⇒a) is the minimal pattern requiring n implications for n statements. Other patterns may suffice. Each implication can be proved by direct, contrapositive or contradiction. Example: the six equivalent characterizations of invertibility of an n×n matrix; prove each implication to complete the cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove existential statements (∃x R(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x R(x) is true you must find and display a specific object x for which R(x) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concrete example and verify it satisfies the required property. Examples: show 2 is an even prime; demonstrate 1729 is expressible as sum of two cubes in two ways. Note: sometimes verification requires a short computation to show the example indeed works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning about existence vs universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an example suffices to prove an existence statement, a single example does not prove a universal/conditional statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse demonstrating one witness for an existential claim with proving that all elements satisfy a property. The text explicitly warns students to avoid this fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proof inside a conditional (constructing witnesses depending on parameters)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an existence statement appears inside a conditional (e.g., 'If a,b ∈ N then ∃k,ℓ ∈ Z such that gcd(a,b)=ak + bℓ'), in a direct proof you assume the antecedent and then produce the witnesses depending on those assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example method: consider the set A = {ax + by : x,y ∈ Z}, take its smallest positive element d, and show d = gcd(a,b) by division algorithm arguments. This constructs k,ℓ explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove uniqueness (there is a unique x with P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness you must (1) produce an example d with P(d) true, and (2) show that any d' with P(d') must equal d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show d = gcd(a,b) has the property and any d' with the same property must equal d by showing d' divides a and b and d divides d', thereby deducing equality. Typical two-part pattern: existence + uniqueness argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive versus non-constructive existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive proofs display an explicit example; non-constructive proofs show that some example exists without exhibiting which one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a non-constructive proof that there exist irrational x,y with x^y rational by a case analysis on (√2)^√2; a constructive proof exhibits explicit x (√2) and y (log_2 3) and proves y is irrational (often by contradiction). Note that non-constructive proofs can show existence without telling which case holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical equivalence used in contradiction for conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the logical equivalence ¬(P⇒Q) ⇔ (P ∧ ¬Q) to set up a contradiction proof for conditionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the equivalence explicit when using contradiction to avoid improper assumptions. The text uses this to justify starting a contradiction-proof of P⇒Q by assuming P and ¬Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove membership a ∈ {x : P(x)}
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a ∈ {x : P(x)} show P(a) is true. For sets of the form {x ∈ S : P(x)}, also verify a ∈ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definition of set-builder notation: elements are exactly those satisfying the predicate. Examples: to show 21 ∈ {x ∈ N : 7|x} show 21∈N and 7|21; to show an ordered pair belongs to {(x,y) ∈ Z×Z : x = y (mod 5)} compute the difference and show it's divisible by 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove A ⊆ B (direct approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A ⊆ B, use direct proof: assume a ∈ A and deduce a ∈ B; thus show 'if a ∈ A then a ∈ B' holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard and usually most straightforward approach. Examples: show multiples of 18 are multiples of 6 by writing a = 18c = 6(3c), deducing 6|a.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove A ⊆ B (contrapositive approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatively, prove the contrapositive: assume a ∉ B and deduce a ∉ A, thereby concluding A ⊆ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach can be more convenient when directly showing a ∈ B is awkward. The text notes both methods are valid and sometimes one is more expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for subset relations
rubrics_metrics.description: You may also prove A ⊆ B by contradiction: assume there exists a with a ∈ A and a ∉ B and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is less commonly needed but is a valid technique; the text mentions it as an option alongside direct and contrapositive approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using cases when proving set containment or membership
rubrics_metrics.description: When the hypothesis is a disjunction (e.g., X ∈ P(A) ∪ P(B) means X ⊆ A or X ⊆ B), handle separate cases to show the required conclusion (e.g., X ⊆ A∪B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove P(A) ∪ P(B) ⊆ P(A ∪ B), consider case X ⊆ A (then X ⊆ A∪B) and case X ⊆ B (then X ⊆ A∪B). Avoid redundant casework by noting overlapping situations are covered by either case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving element inclusion from equality of power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(A) = P(B), then A ⊆ B (and similarly B ⊆ A), because every singleton {a} ∈ P(A) must lie in P(B), hence {a} ⊆ B and therefore a ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: take an arbitrary a ∈ A, note {a} ∈ P(A) = P(B), so {a} ∈ P(B) meaning {a} ⊆ B, hence a ∈ B. This gives a clean way to deduce subset inclusion from equality of power sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental verification vs formal proof of obvious set identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subset relations (e.g., A∩B ⊆ A, A ⊆ A∪B, A−B ⊆ A) are obvious enough that the reader may accept them without formal proof, though quick mental proofs are recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text advises not to waste time proving trivial facts unless explicitly asked, but encourages students to be able to mentally justify such relations to avoid misunderstandings.
